scenario.speaker: dana
scenario.briefing:
**Neo Smart Living's focus groups are on the calendar** — four sessions across Southern California, including one in the Inland Empire — and the professional moderator we hired, **Renee**, will run every one of them from the guide *you* build. Renee is excellent, but a moderator can only be as good as the script she's handed.

The stakes: Neo has to decide how to **position, feature, and price the Tahoe Mini**, and these groups feed all three decisions. That means your question set has to cover the full arc — how homeowners use their yards today, what they know about backyard units, competitor impressions, must-have features, use cases, price expectations, the language that sells or scares, and the barriers that stop a purchase.

Here's how the builder works: Marcus assembled a bank of candidate content — introduction parts, icebreakers, discussion questions, and group activities, each with an estimated running time. You assemble the guide from it: one option for each of the **six introduction parts** (including how to handle money talk), **one icebreaker**, **nine discussion questions**, and **three activities**. Quality and timing both count — every choice adds its minutes to the session. Target length: **60 minutes**, and Renee will hold you to it.

My memo, Neo's discussion objectives, and condensed versions of the round-4 articles are in your Inbox and Resources. There's also a guide on asking about price without anchoring — read it before you touch the question bank.

inbox.subject: Neo's moderator's guide — this one travels
inbox.body:
Before anything else, here's why I care about this document more than almost any other in qualitative work: **the guide is the study**. A survey can be tightened after a soft launch; a focus group happens once, live, in front of the client. If the guide leads participants, they'll perform agreement instead of giving opinions. If it skips the ground rules, one loud voice will own the room. If it runs long, the moderator will cut the activities — usually where the best material surfaces — to make up time.

We've contracted **Renee Calloway** to moderate Neo Smart Living's four focus groups — three across coastal SoCal metros and one in the **Inland Empire**, where lots are bigger and budgets run differently. Renee moderates from the guide, word for word where it counts. Whatever you put on the page happens four times, in front of the client, on video. Whatever you leave out never happens at all.

Work backward from Neo's decisions: **positioning** (what the Tahoe Mini should mean to buyers), **features** (what the standard build must include), and **price** (whether the current number holds). The guide has to earn all three without ever tipping Neo's hand — participants must not learn the client's name, and above all, nobody in that room says Neo's price out loud. The moment a moderator names a number, every reaction that follows is a reaction to that number. Get expectations out of participants' own heads; the guide library has a new entry on exactly how.

One more thing: money talk makes strangers clam up. Your introduction now includes a sensitive-topic section — set it up so people can discuss budgets comfortably, in ranges, with permission to pass.

Neo's discussion objectives are attached. The condensed secondary-research articles from round 4 are in Resources — your competitor and price-expectation questions should be informed by them. Marcus reviews the build.

— Dana

attachments.title: Neo Smart Living — Discussion Objectives
attachments.body:
**Client.** Neo Smart Living designs and installs compact, factory-built backyard units in Southern California. Its lead product, the **Tahoe Mini**, is a 117-square-foot (9 ft × 13 ft) structure delivered and installed in about a day: pre-wired electrical, smart entry lock, dual-pane floor-to-ceiling glass, and a pitched roof with drainage, with options for sound insulation, heating and cooling, and privacy panel swaps. Neo's catalog also includes the **Mojave**, an expandable container tiny home — up to 400 square feet expanded, with a full kitchen and bathroom, advertised at $35,800. **The Mojave is out of scope for these groups:** sessions must stay on the backyard-studio category, and the moderator must not introduce the Mojave, the Tahoe Mini, or any Neo price by name. It is deliberately **not an ADU**: no plumbing, no kitchen — a non-habitable accessory structure sized under California's roughly 120-square-foot permit threshold, so most installations need no building permit (HOA and local rules still apply).

**Decisions this research feeds.** (1) **Positioning** — which use cases and messages should lead: home office, wellness or hobby space, guest space, or something else. (2) **Features** — which elements belong in the standard build versus the options list, with particular attention to privacy, climate comfort, and interior fit-out. (3) **Price** — whether the current price point is defensible, and what homeowners expect a unit like this to cost. The moderator must never disclose Neo's price or name the client.

**Discussion coverage required.** Current backyard use; awareness and consideration of backyard units; impressions of competitors in the category; must-have features; use-case framing; price expectations elicited without anchoring; reaction to concept language such as factory-built versus prefab; purchase barriers including HOA and permit concerns; and a closing synthesis of priorities.

**Participants.** Owner-occupied single-family homeowners in Southern California with usable yard space, ages 30–65, household income $75,000 or more, interested in flexible space for remote work, wellness, or guests.

**Sessions.** Four groups of 8–10, professionally moderated, recorded; one group in the Inland Empire. Guides should be built to run in **60 minutes**.

inbox.subject: The bar for this one
inbox.body:
My standing checklist for any moderator's guide: neutral introduction, consent on tape, on-topic icebreaker, broad-to-narrow funnel, activities that use the group as a group, minutes that add up. Three additions for Neo:

1. **Nine questions have to carry three decisions.** Positioning, features, price. Before you lock the set, walk the arc: yard today → awareness → competitors → must-haves → use cases → price expectations → concept language → barriers → synthesis. If one of those beats is missing, a client decision goes into the report unsupported.
2. **Price without anchoring.** The transcript from these groups will feed our pricing recommendation, so the expectation question has to come from participants' own heads. If a question in the bank names a dollar figure, that figure is all four groups will talk about. Read the new guide entry before you pick.
3. **Words are stimuli too.** Neo says factory-built; the category says prefab; homeowners hear something by each. There should be a question that tests the language itself.

One scope note: Neo's catalog also includes the Mojave — a 400-square-foot expandable tiny home with a kitchen and bathroom. These groups are about the Tahoe Mini and the studio category. If a candidate question drags the room into plumbed-tiny-home territory — or worse, names the client's products or prices — it doesn't belong in the guide.

And the math: Renee runs a tight room, and the facility bills by the hour. Sixty minutes, not sixty-something.

— Marcus

pages.title: Neo Smart Living Moderator's Guide Builder
pages.intro: Assemble the moderator's guide Renee will use in all four Neo Smart Living groups. Pick **one option in each of the six introduction parts**, **one icebreaker**, **nine discussion questions**, and **three activities**. Each option shows its running time — the session should total exactly **60 minutes**.

tasks.title: Create Neo Smart Living's Moderator's Guide
tasks.prompt: Build the guide section by section. The nine questions must cover the full discussion arc Neo's objectives require — and the session has to run in the booked hour.

timeBudget.label: Session length
timeBudget.idealNote: a well-run session comes in right at 60 minutes

sections.label: Introduction
sections.note: Pick one option for each of the six parts of the introduction.

options.text: "Good evening — thanks for being here. I'm Renee, your moderator. My job is to ask questions, watch the clock, and make sure everyone gets heard. I don't work for any company whose products we might discuss, and nothing you say tonight affects me either way — honest opinions are the whole point."

"Welcome! Tonight's session is sponsored by Neo Smart Living, the Southern California company behind the Tahoe Mini backyard studio. They're deciding how to take their product to the next level, and you're going to help them do it!"

"Hi everyone, I'm Renee. I've worked around the backyard-structure business for years, so I know this category inside and out — if you're not sure what to think about something tonight, just ask me and I'll give you the industry view."

"Tonight we're going to talk about your home and your yard — how you use your outdoor space, and your reactions to some ideas about flexible space at home. A company will use what you share to make product decisions. There are no right or wrong answers; we want your honest experiences and opinions, whatever they are."
"Tonight we're going to explore why backyard studios have become the smartest investment a Southern California homeowner can make, and hear about all the ways one would improve your daily life."

"A few ground rules. One voice at a time, for the recording. There are no wrong answers, and please disagree with each other — different views are exactly what we need. If I move us along, that's the clock talking, not a judgment. I'll make sure everyone gets airtime, so don't be surprised if I call on you. Phones on silent, please."
"A quick rule for tonight: groups like this work best when we find common ground, so as each topic comes up, try to reach a consensus the whole table can agree on before we move to the next one."
"Ground rules: no interrupting, no rambling, no personal stories unless I ask for one, and keep your answers brief — we have a lot to cover and I intend to finish on time."

"Before we start: tonight's session is being audio- and video-recorded, and members of the research team are observing. Recordings are used only for research; your names are removed from all reports and nothing is ever tied to you personally. Is everyone comfortable proceeding? Please say yes out loud for the recording."
"You'll see cameras in the corners — standard facility equipment, nothing to think about. Pretend they're not there and let's jump in."

"Later tonight we'll talk about budgets and what things cost. To be clear up front: nobody will ask about your personal finances. We'll talk in general ranges about what products seem worth, there are no right answers, and if any question isn't comfortable, just say pass — that's always fine."

"Later we'll get into money, and precision really matters for the research — so when we do, please be ready to share your household income, what you paid for your home, and exactly what you could afford to spend on a project like this."
"One promise: we will not talk about money tonight. Price conversations make groups uncomfortable, so if costs come up I'll steer us to a different topic."

"We'll start easy — just talking about your homes and yards — and work toward specific ideas later in the hour. You're the expert on your own house and how your family lives in it, so speak from your own experience, and feel free to build on what you hear."
"We're on a tight clock tonight, so let's skip the warm-up chatter and go straight to the product ideas — we'll get to know each other as we go."

sections.label: Icebreaker
sections.note: Pick one icebreaker to open the discussion.

options.text: "Let's go around the room: tell us your first name, and describe your backyard and how you use it today."
"Let's go around the room: tell us your first name and the best thing you did last weekend."
"Let's get acquainted: go around and tell the group roughly what your home is worth today and how much equity you've built up in it."

sections.label: Discussion questions
sections.note: Pick nine questions. Together they must cover the full arc: yard use, awareness, competitors, features, use cases, price expectations, concept language, barriers, and synthesis.

options.text: "Walk me through your backyard as it is today — what's out there, and how does your household actually use the space week to week?"
"Have you ever looked into adding a structure to your yard — a studio, office, shed, or something else? What got you thinking about it, and how far did you get?"
"What companies or products come to mind when you think about backyard studios or prefab structures? What have you seen or heard about them — good or bad?"
"If you were designing a backyard studio for your own family, what would it absolutely have to have? Probe: privacy, staying cool in summer and warm in winter, and how the inside is finished."
"Imagine the structure showed up in your yard tomorrow, finished. What would it become — a workspace, a wellness or hobby room, a guest space, something else? Walk me through a typical week with it."

"Inspired by what we've been describing — a finished, insulated backyard studio with electricity, installed in a day — what would you expect something like that to cost? What price would feel like a bargain, and what price would feel like too much?"
"When I say a structure is 'factory-built', what does that suggest to you about it? What about 'prefab'? Do those words make it more appealing, less appealing, or neither?"
"What could get in the way of actually adding something like this to your yard — think HOA rules, permits, neighbors, space, anything else?"
"Last one: of everything we discussed tonight, what's the one thing the product team should remember? If you were them, what would you build or change first?"
"Wouldn't you agree that a backyard office would completely transform your work-from-home life?"
"How do you feel about the price and the installation process of backyard studios?"
"Do you want a backyard studio?"
"How does the distinction between a habitable ADU and a non-habitable accessory structure below the permit threshold affect your purchase calculus?"
"One company sells a 117-square-foot backyard unit for $23,000, delivered and installed. Does that sound fair to you?"
"Just for fun — what do you know about the history of prefabricated housing in America? Any famous examples come to mind?"
"If money were absolutely no object, describe the ultimate luxury backyard compound you would build — pools, guest houses, anything."
"Tell me about your ideal home office — anywhere in the house. What would it look like and what would be in it?"
"Be honest — would your neighbors be jealous if a beautiful studio appeared in your backyard?"

"The company behind tonight's concept, Neo Smart Living, also sells the Mojave — a 400-square-foot expandable tiny home with a full kitchen and bathroom for $35,800. Would you rather buy that instead?"

sections.label: Group activities
sections.note: Pick three activities for the back half of the session.

options.text: Feature card-sort — In pairs, participants sort feature cards (privacy glass, sound insulation, heating and cooling, desk and shelving fit-out, smart lock, and more) into must-have, nice-to-have, and no-thanks piles, then defend their toughest calls to the group.

Price-ladder exercise — Each participant fills in their own blank ladder for a finished backyard studio: the price that would feel too cheap to trust, a bargain, getting expensive, and too expensive to consider. Participants write their own numbers first, then the group compares ladders and talks through the gaps.

Floor-plan sketch — Each participant sketches the interior of their ideal unit on a blank 9-by-13 outline — furniture, windows, door — then gives the group a 30-second tour. A projective exercise that reveals the use case people actually picture.

Individual essay — Participants set the discussion aside and spend the block silently writing a one-page essay on what flexible space at home means to them, working alone without talking, papers collected at the end.
Competitor-ad screening — The moderator plays a reel of backyard-structure commercials and social ads, and the group critiques each brand's advertising style, spokespeople, and slogans.

guides.title: Anatomy of a Moderator's Guide
guides.body:
A moderator's guide is the script for a focus group — not word-for-word, but a plan the moderator can run under pressure. Nearly every good guide has the same skeleton:

1. **Introduction (~10 min).** Five jobs, in order: a *welcome* that establishes the moderator as a neutral host; a *purpose* statement that explains why everyone is here without revealing the client (once people know the brand, they perform for it); *ground rules* that invite disagreement and share the floor; a *recording disclosure* that tells participants they're being recorded and observed, promises confidentiality, and asks for consent; and a *warm-up framing* that lowers the stakes — no test, no wrong answers, start with their world. When the discussion will touch sensitive ground (money, health, family), add a sixth element that sets expectations: general ranges, no personal disclosures required, passing is always allowed.
2. **Icebreaker (5–8 min).** One easy question everyone answers. The best icebreakers are low-stakes *and* on-topic: they get every voice in the room early and point the conversation at the subject.
3. **Question funnel (20–30 min).** Broad to narrow. Start with current behavior and experiences (their world), move to needs and ideas, and only then present specific directions for reaction. Starting narrow contaminates everything after it.
4. **Activities (15–20 min).** One or two structured exercises — sorting, ranking, drawing, building. Activities pull contributions from quieter participants and produce artifacts you can analyze later. They belong in the back half, once trust is built.
5. **Close (a few minutes).** Final thoughts, thanks, incentives, dismissal.

**Timing discipline.** Most professional groups are booked for about an hour; a guide that plans **~55–60 minutes of content** leaves margin for late arrivals and long answers. Attention sags past the hour, and recruiters promised participants a specific commitment. Write a minutes number next to every element, add them up, and cut until the total fits. A guide that doesn't fit forces the moderator to improvise cuts live — and the activities, often the most valuable part, are what get cut.

**In this assignment:** every option shows its estimated minutes and the builder shows your running total. The client's brief tells you the target. Treat the total as part of the deliverable, because it is.

guides.title: Writing Questions That Open People Up
guides.body:
A focus group lives or dies on question wording. The same topic, asked two ways, produces either a conversation or a row of nodding heads. The classic flaws:

- **Leading questions** embed the desired answer. "You'd love a bigger studio, right?" tells participants what to say; agreeing is easier than arguing. Fix: ask for experience, not agreement — "Tell me about a time extra space would have mattered."
- **Double-barreled questions** ask two things at once. "How do you feel about the price and the quality?" gets you an answer to one of them and you won't know which. Fix: one idea per question.
- **Yes/no dead-ends** close the conversation. "Do you want one?" earns a "yes" and silence. Fix: start with how, what, walk me through, tell me about.
- **Jargon** makes participants feel tested. Technical or regulatory terms the client uses internally mean nothing in the room — people either bluff or go quiet. Fix: everyday words, or define the term before asking about it.
- **Premature price hypotheticals.** "Would you pay $X?" asked before people have explored the product produces guesses, not evidence — and the number you name becomes an anchor that skews everything after it. Price talk belongs late, and it should start from the participant's own expectations, not a number you supply.

Two more habits of good discussion questions: they ask about **specific, recent experiences** rather than generalities ("tell me about the last time…"), and they leave the moderator **room to probe** ("what makes that the one?"). If a question can be answered in one word by a bored person, rewrite it.

**For this round:** the question set also has to *cover the client's decisions*. Before locking nine questions, check the arc — current behavior, awareness, competitors, features, use cases, price expectations, concept language, barriers, synthesis. A flawless question that duplicates a beat you already covered is worth less than a plain one that covers a beat you missed.

guides.title: Asking About Price Without Anchoring
guides.body:
Price is the easiest topic to ruin in qualitative research, because of **anchoring**: the first number spoken in the room becomes the reference point for every judgment that follows. If the moderator says "one company charges $20,000," the group spends the rest of the night reacting to $20,000 — not telling you what they'd expect to pay. The anchor doesn't even have to be relevant; any number pulls estimates toward itself.

Rules for the price section of a guide:

1. **The moderator never names a number first.** Not the client's price, not a competitor's price, not a "for example" price. If a participant names one, fine — that's data. Sourced from them, it's evidence; sourced from you, it's contamination.
2. **Ask late in the funnel.** Price expectations mean nothing until participants have a concrete picture of the product — features, quality, installation. Let them build that picture first, then ask what *something like that* should cost.
3. **Elicit a range, not a verdict.** One number per person hides the structure of their expectations. Better: ask where a price would start to feel like a *bargain*, where it starts feeling *expensive*, and where it becomes *too expensive to consider*. (Quantitative pricing research formalizes this with a four-question technique; in a group, the informal version works fine.) A blank price-ladder each participant fills in privately — before anyone speaks — protects against participants anchoring each other.
4. **Frame it as expectations, not means-testing.** "What would you expect a product like this to cost?" is comfortable. "What can you afford?" is not, and it's a different question anyway. The sensitive-topic framing in your introduction sets this contract; the price question has to honor it.

One warning sign to check in any question bank: if a candidate price question already contains a dollar sign, it anchors. There's a difference between *asking about* price and *telling* the room a price and grading their reaction.

resources.title: Backyard Studios, Space Pods, and Expandable Tiny Homes: A Category Field Guide (condensed)
resources.body: *Structure & Site Quarterly, condensed.* Two products share the backyard, and the legal line between them is the ADU definition: complete independent living facilities — living, sleeping, eating, cooking, sanitation (California Gov. Code § 66313). **Finished studios and pods (no plumbing, often no permit):** the reference product is the **Autonomous WorkPod** — 102 sq ft, advertised at **$20,900** DIY, insulation standard, single-cable power hookup, direct online purchase with published reviews. **Studio Home's Signature Series** (96–192 sq ft, from about **$18,000**) competes on a configurator with installation and interiors priced separately; **Modern Shed** sells consultant-led bespoke studios, quote-only, with California installer support; **Kanga Room Systems'** Modern Kwik Room 10×12 (120 sq ft) is the kit benchmark — **$18,900** as a shell, **$40,600** turnkey in its Texas-only program. **Expandable homes and foldable ADUs (kitchen + bath, ADU-capable):** **Bright Box Homes** from $35,995; **Elite Nest 400** from $16,999 with a "95% complete" claim and thin documentation; **BOXABL's Casita** at ~$60,000 unit-only or ~$150,000 California turnkey. The analyst's rule: buyers cross-shop within a category — a $16,999 expandable dwelling is not a cheap studio.

resources.title: Backyard-Unit Buyer Trends by Homeowner Segment (condensed)
resources.body: Purchase interest in backyard units concentrates among owner-occupied single-family homeowners with usable yard space, with the strongest engagement between ages 30 and 65 and household incomes above $75K. Three demand stories dominate. **Remote and hybrid workers** want a dedicated office separated from the house — the segment most willing to pay for insulation, climate control, and desk-ready fit-out. **Wellness and hobby buyers** — home gyms, yoga and music rooms, studios — are the fastest-growing segment and respond to light, privacy, and finished interiors. **Guest-space buyers** exist but frequently discover that hosting overnight guests pushes them out of the studio category entirely, into plumbed, ADU-capable units at two to three times the cost. Reported barriers cluster around total cost, uncertainty about HOA rules and permits, and doubts about build quality versus site-built construction. Regionally, inland markets show larger lots and stronger space needs but greater price sensitivity than coastal metros.

resources.title: Opportunities & Forecasts for the North American Compact-Structure Market (condensed)
resources.body: Forecasters expect continued growth in compact accessory structures through the decade, driven by entrenched hybrid work, high costs of home additions, and interest in flexible space. Advertised prices for finished studios in the 100-to-120-square-foot class cluster between **$18,000 and $21,000** — WorkPod at $20,900 with insulation standard, Studio Home from about $18,000 before installation, Kanga at $18,900 for a shell — but the report's central warning is that **advertised prices are not comparable across completion levels**: Kanga's own Texas program reprices its $18,900 shell at $40,600 turnkey. The decision metric is total cost to a legally usable, installed space. The report also flags a structural advantage for units sized under local permit thresholds (about 120 sq ft in California): faster installation, lower soft costs, and a simpler purchase decision — provided buyers understand the structures are non-habitable.
